title: 2. Character Dynamics (Relationship Tropes)
use_cases: Use when designing character arcs and relationship progressions between protagonists
Configure when establishing external and internal narrative conflicts
Implement when selecting a POV structure to highlight specific dynamic tensions
Use when referencing common genre conventions for romance and conflict-driven fiction
Implement when developing character foils to contrast worldviews
content:
#### Romance-Centric

- Enemies to Lovers – Each POV reveals their grudging attraction (e.g., The Worst Best Man by Mia Sosa).
- Fake Dating – One POV is faking it, the other might not be (e.g., To Love Jason Thorn by Ella Maise).
- Miscommunication Angst – Both POVs misinterpret each other’s actions (e.g., The Heart Principle by Helen Hoang).
- Second-Chance Romance – One POV dwells on the past, the other resists (e.g., Every Summer After by Carley Fortune).
- Forced Proximity – Trapped together (e.g., The Darkness Outside Us by Eliot Schrefer).

#### Conflict-Driven

- Opponents to Allies – Like Enemies to Lovers but not driven by romance (e.g., Legend by Marie Lu, This Is How You Lose the Time War by Amal El-Mohtar & Max Gladstone)
- Foil Characters – Contrasting worldviews or attitudes, often in indirect conflict (We Are Not Like Them by Christine Pride & Jo Piazza).
- Betrayer/Betrayed – One POV hides a secret (e.g., Gone Girl by Gillian Flynn).
